original_interpretation: SIA, citing an SIA-Deloitte report, says a single AI server rack contains over 4,500 packaged chips, which make up more than 95% of the rack's content value.
evidence_found: "According to a recent SIA-Deloitte report, within a modern data center a single AI server rack contains over 4,500 packaged chips" and "Semiconductors account for more than 95% of a leading AI server rack's content value" (SIA 2026 SOI, p. 9, 'AI is built on semiconductors'); intro p. 4: "accounting for 95% of its value".
notes: Both figures are on p. 9. The 4,500 figure is explicitly attributed to the SIA-Deloitte report; the 95% sentence follows in the same section without its own attribution. The intro (p. 4) says '95%', p. 9 says 'more than 95%'. These are modelled figures from an industry-body/consultancy study, so 'estimate' fits better than 'reported_claim'.

original_interpretation: In 2025 PC/computers/AI rose to 45.5% of global semiconductor demand, from 35% in 2024 (WSTS End-Use Survey via SIA).
evidence_found: Chart 'TOTAL GLOBAL DEMAND SHARE BY END USE, 2024-2025' (SIA 2026 SOI, p. 8), read from page image and PDF text layer: PC/Computers/AI 35% (2024), 45.5% (2025); "Source: WSTS, End-Use Survey, various years". Text: "End-use share by revenue grew by more than 10% for computers and AI applications".
notes: I checked the values against both the PDF text layer and a render of the page image. The 2024 values are whole numbers, the 2025 values have one decimal. The 'more than 10%' in the text is +10.5 percentage points. claim_type fact is acceptable: this is WSTS survey data republished by an industry body.

original_interpretation: In 2025 communications fell to 28.7% of global semiconductor demand, automotive to 10.9%, consumer electronics to 7%, industrial to 7% and government to 0.9%.
evidence_found: Same chart (SIA 2026 SOI, p. 8), 2024 to 2025: Communications 33% to 28.7%; Automotive 13% to 10.9%; Consumer Electronics 10% to 7%; Industrial Applications 8% to 7%; Government 1% to 0.9%.
notes: Every value matches the page text layer and the page image. Both years sum to 100%.

original_interpretation: SIA states that communications, auto, consumer electronics, industrial and government chip sales all grew in value in 2025 but each lost share because of AI-driven growth.
evidence_found: "Even as semiconductor sales for communications, auto, consumer electronics, industrial applications, and government end uses grew in value in 2025, each accounted for a smaller share of overall semiconductor sales due to the explosive growth in semiconductor demand from AI." (SIA 2026 SOI, p. 8). WSTS: 2025 sales US$795.6bn, +26.2% (SRC-0428).
correction: SIA does make this statement, but its own rounded shares do not support 'grew in value' for consumer electronics. 10% of the 2024 total (~US$630bn, implied by WSTS's US$795.6bn at +26.2%) is ~US$63bn; 7% of US$795.6bn is ~US$56bn. Even at the rounding limits (9.5% vs 7.49%) the value falls slightly. Communications (~+10%), automotive (~+6%), industrial (~+10%) and government (~+14%) do grow on these shares.
notes: The statement is accurately attributed to SIA. The arithmetic is mine: shares from the p. 8 chart, totals from the WSTS release. WSTS's own release reports growth only for Computer (>60%), Government (15%) and Industrial (5%).

original_interpretation: In 2023 communications took US$169.2bn of chip demand (-1.8%), computer US$140.0bn (-7.1%), automotive US$90.1bn (+15.0%), industrial US$72.1bn (-13.3%), consumer US$54.8bn (-31.9%) and government US$5.0bn (-45.0%); automotive was the only segment that grew.
evidence_found: Table 'GLOBAL DEMAND BY END USE, 2023' (SIA 2024 SOI, p. 24), from page image: Communication -1.8 / 169.2; Computer -7.1 / 140.0; Automotive 15.0 / 90.1; Consumer -31.9 / 54.8; Industrial -13.3 / 72.1; Government -45.0 / 5.0. Text: "the automotive sector experienced the largest growth in share of chip sales to become the third-largest end market in 2023."
notes: All values match. Automotive is the only positive growth rate in the table. The table has no source line, so the WSTS End Use Survey methodology in metric is the researcher's attribution, not printed on the page. The segments sum to US$531.2bn, versus US$526.8bn total 2023 sales in SIA's Feb 2024 release (SRC-0055).

original_interpretation: In 2022 communications took US$172.3bn of chip demand (+1.0%), computer US$150.7bn (-13.9%), industrial US$83.1bn (+24.2%), consumer US$80.5bn (+17.7%), automotive US$78.3bn (+13.4%) and government US$9.1bn (+56.5%).
evidence_found: Table '2022 DEMAND BY END-USE' (SIA 2023 SOI, printed p. 18), from page image and text layer: Communication 1.0 / 172.3; Computer -13.9 / 150.7; Industrial 24.2 / 83.1; Consumer 17.7 / 80.5; Automotive 13.4 / 78.3; Government 56.5 / 9.1.
notes: All values match. The growth figures have no % sign on the page. There is no source line under the table, so the WSTS methodology attribution is the researcher's. The segments sum to US$574.0bn, matching the US$574.1bn 2022 total on p. 16.

original_interpretation: In 2020 the computer end use took US$142.2bn (+21.2%) of global chip demand, communications US$137.6bn (+1.2%), consumer US$53.0bn (-3.0%), industrial US$52.9bn (+8.2%), automotive US$50.1bn (-0.3%) and government US$4.6bn (-11.8%).
evidence_found: Table '2020 DEMAND BY END-USE' (SIA 2021 SOI, p. 12), from page image and text layer: Computer 21.2 / 142.2; Communication 1.2 / 137.6; Consumer -3.0 / 53.0; Industrial 8.2 / 52.9; Automotive -0.3 / 50.1; Government -11.8 / 4.6.
notes: All values match. As the researcher noted, there is no source line under the table.

original_interpretation: In 2023 MPUs were US$45.3 billion (-10.9%), MCUs US$27.9 billion (+11.4%) and DSPs US$3.2 billion (-1.4%) of worldwide sales (SIA Factbook).
evidence_found: 2024 Factbook p. 9 ('Section 2: Global Market - 9 -', PDF p. 12) chart: MPU $45.3B -10.9%; MCU $27.9B +11.4%; DSP $3.2B -1.4%. Text: "In 2023, these products accounted for 75 percent". SIA release 5 Feb 2024: "Microcontroller units (MCUs) grew by 11.4% to a total of $27.9 billion."
notes: The chart title says 'By Product Segment 2022', but the body text and values are 2023: the segments total ~US$526.9bn and memory is US$92.3bn (-28.9%), matching SRC-0055. The printed page is 9, not 12; 12 is the PDF page.

original_interpretation: SIA states that logic, memory, analog and MPU accounted for 75% of semiconductor sales in 2023, down from 79% in 2021, as memory fell to US$92.3 billion.
evidence_found: 2024 Factbook printed p. 9: "In recent years, the largest segments ... have been logic, memory, analog, and MPU. In 2023, these products accounted for 75 percent of semiconductor industry sales." Chart: Logic $178.6B, Memory $92.3B (-28.9%), Analog $81.2B, MPU $45.3B. 2022 Factbook printed p. 12: "In 2021, these products accounted for 79 percent".
correction: The 75% (2023) and memory US$92.3bn figures are verified. 'Down from 79% in 2021' comes from a different document (the 2022 Factbook), and the causal 'as memory fell' is our reading: SIA does not state either in the 2024 Factbook.
notes: The four segments sum to US$397.4bn of US$526.9bn, which is 75.4%, consistent with the text.

original_interpretation: SIA's 2024 Factbook gives 2023 end-use shares of communications 32%, PC/computer 25%, automotive 17.0%, industrial 14.0%, consumer 11.0% and government 1.0%.
evidence_found: Pie '2023 Total Global Semiconductor Market: $526.9 Billion' (2024 Factbook, printed p. 8, PDF p. 11), from page image: Communications 32%, PC/Computer 25%, Automotive 17.0%, Industrial 14.0%, Consumer 11.0%, Government 1.0%; "Note: Military end-use is included in Government. Sources: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS)."
notes: The label-to-value mapping was confirmed from the rendered image. The text layer lists the values without labels. The shares implied by the SIA 2024 SOI US$ table (SRC-0422) are close but not identical: Comm 31.9, Computer 26.4, Auto 17.0, Industrial 13.6, Consumer 10.3, Gov 0.9. The printed page is 8, not 11.

original_interpretation: SIA put 2021 worldwide logic sales at US$154.8 billion (+30.8%) and memory at US$153.8 billion (+30.9%), the two largest product segments.
evidence_found: Chart 'Distribution of Worldwide Semiconductor Sales By Product Segment 2021' (2022 Factbook, printed p. 12, PDF p. 15), read from page image (the text layer is garbled): Logic $154.8B +30.8%; Memory $153.8B +30.9%; "Source: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) and SIA Estimates."
notes: Values match. These are the two largest of the nine segments shown.

original_interpretation: In 2021 MPUs were US$57.8 billion, MCUs US$19.6 billion and DSPs US$2.8 billion of worldwide sales (SIA Factbook).
evidence_found: Same chart (2022 Factbook, printed p. 12), from page image: MPU $57.8B +11.5%; MCU $19.6B +26.7%; DSP $2.8B +19.4%.

original_interpretation: SIA states that logic, memory, analog and MPU together accounted for 79% of semiconductor sales in 2021.
evidence_found: 2022 Factbook printed p. 12: "In recent years, the largest segments of the worldwide semiconductor industry have been memory, logic, analog, and MPU. In 2021, these products accounted for 79 percent of semiconductor industry sales."
notes: Arithmetic check: 154.8+153.8+74.1+57.8 = US$440.5bn of ~US$555.7bn is 79.3%. The quote was read from the page image because the PDF text layer is garbled.

original_interpretation: In 2021 WSTS end-use shares were PC/computer 31.5%, communications 30.7%, automotive 12.4%, consumer 12.3%, industrial 12.0% and government 1.0% of a US$556bn market.
evidence_found: Pie '2021 Total Global Semiconductor Market: $556 Billion Percent of Semiconductor Demand, by End Use' (2022 Factbook, printed p. 11, PDF p. 14), from page image: PC/Computer 31.5%, Communications 30.7%, Automotive 12.4%, Consumer 12.3%, Industrial 12.0%, Government 1.0%; "Sources: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS)."
notes: Values match; they sum to 99.9% because of rounding.

original_interpretation: The WSTS End-Use Survey classifies product-category dollar shipments by end use and region; it is filled by WSTS members that choose to take part, plus an allocation for non-participants in the Blue Book.
evidence_found: "The survey is based on total product category shipments, in dollars, classified by end use in various geographic sectors." ... "This data is gathered by the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) organization and its member companies that elect to participate in the survey, plus an allocation for the amounts estimated for non-participants included in the WSTS 'Blue Book' report for 2025." (SIA End Use Survey page)

original_interpretation: SIA sells the WSTS End-Use Survey separately for US$350; it is not included in the regular WSTS statistics subscription, and the current data set covers January-December 2025.
evidence_found: "Purchase the End Use Survey now for $350"; "The current data set covers January 2025 through December 2025."; "The End-Use Survey is not available through a regular Statistics Subscription." (SIA End Use Survey page, re-opened 2026-10-01)
notes: Price and coverage were current as of 2026-10-01; the page has no date. The page says 'Statistics Subscription' and does not specifically say 'WSTS'.

original_interpretation: WSTS states that the logic category's 2025 growth was driven by high-performance chips for data centers and AI accelerators, which places AI accelerators within WSTS logic.
evidence_found: WSTS release: "Logic devices delivered the largest contribution to overall market expansion, supported by demand for high-performance chips used in data centers, AI accelerators, and advanced computing systems." WSTS Product Classification 2021 p. 13: ICs "having multiple functional cores including MPU-, MCU- or DSP-core, are NOT to be reported in this MOS Micro category, but ... under appropriate MOS Logic categories (code L)".
correction: WSTS says logic made the largest contribution to growth, 'supported by' demand for chips used in data centers and AI accelerators. That AI accelerators are classified within WSTS logic is our inference, not a WSTS statement. It is consistent with the classification rule that multi-core ICs are reported under MOS Logic (SRC-0004 p. 13).
notes: The second half of the claim is an inference, so claim_type 'reported_claim' does not fit it. Better: split it into a fact (WSTS statement) and an inference (classification). SRC-0004 is the 2021 issue of the classification.

original_interpretation: WSTS reports that its Computer end-market segment grew more than 60% in 2025, government-related demand 15% and industrial 5%.
evidence_found: "2025 growth was primarily driven by the Computer Segment, which expanded by more than 60 percent year-over-year." ... "Government-related demand increased by 15 percent ... The Industrial segment returned to growth with an increase of 5 percent" (WSTS full-year 2025 release, 'End-market segments')
notes: Consistent with the SIA 2026 SOI shares (SRC-0421): 35% of ~US$630bn growing to 45.5% of US$795.6bn is about +64%. The release does not name the End Use Survey as the method; metric.methodology is the researcher's attribution.

original_interpretation: Gartner's public forecast tables split semiconductor revenue only into memory and non-memory; finer device categories are available only to clients.
evidence_found: Gartner release 24 Aug 2026: "Table 1: Semiconductor Revenue Forecast, Worldwide, 2025-2027 (Billions in U.S. Dollars)" rows Memory / Nonmemory / Total Market; same release text: "DRAM revenue is forecast to increase 246.6% in 2026, while NAND flash revenue is expected to grow 371.9%"; "Gartner clients can read more in Forecast: Semiconductors and Electronics, Worldwide, 2024-2030, 2Q26."
correction: Only this release's Table 1 is checked here, and it splits memory/non-memory. The same public release also gives DRAM and NAND growth and an AI data-center share. So 'only into memory and non-memory' overstates. 'Finer categories available only to clients' is inferred from the client-report pointer, not stated.
notes: This generalises from one release to all of 'Gartner's public forecast tables'.

original_interpretation: Gartner (August 2026) forecasts memory revenue of US$837.3bn in 2026 (54% of the market, up from 27% in 2025) and non-memory revenue of US$717.9bn, up 21.9% from US$589.0bn.
evidence_found: "Memory revenue is forecast to total $837 billion in 2026 ... forecast to account for 54% of total semiconductor revenue, up from 27% in 2025"; Table 1: Memory 220.1 / 837.3 / 1,075.5; Nonmemory 589.0 / 717.9 / 864.4; "Excluding memory, Gartner forecasts semiconductor revenue to grow from $589 billion in 2025 to $718 billion in 2026, an increase of 21.9%" (Gartner, 24 Aug 2026)
notes: These are forecasts, correctly typed as estimate. 837.3/1,555.2 is 53.8%.

original_interpretation: Gartner's August 2026 release puts 2025 memory revenue at US$220.1bn within a US$809.0bn total market.
evidence_found: Table 1, 2025 column: "Memory 220.1 ... Nonmemory 589.0 ... Total Market 809.0"; text: "increasing 92% from 2025 revenue of $809 billion" (Gartner, 24 Aug 2026)
notes: This is Gartner's vendor-revenue basis. It differs from WSTS (US$795.6bn total; memory US$230.0bn in the SIA 2026 SOI p. 6). The two measure different populations, so this is not a contradiction.

original_interpretation: Gartner forecasts 2026 DRAM revenue growth of 246.6% and NAND flash growth of 371.9%, and attributes the year's acceleration to a 'stronger-than-anticipated memory pricing cycle' as well as AI investment.
evidence_found: "DRAM revenue is forecast to increase 246.6% in 2026, while NAND flash revenue is expected to grow 371.9%." Ben Lee: "The pace of industry expansion is accelerating dramatically, driven by sustained investment in AI infrastructure and a stronger-than-anticipated memory pricing cycle." (Gartner, 24 Aug 2026)

original_interpretation: Gartner expects the AI data-center ecosystem to grow from 36.5% of semiconductor revenue in 2026 to more than 53% by 2030.
evidence_found: Ben Lee quote: "The AI data center ecosystem is expected to grow from 36.5% of the semiconductor revenue in 2026 to more than 53% by 2030, underscoring a structural shift in where semiconductor value is created" (Gartner, 24 Aug 2026)
notes: Gartner gives no definition of 'AI data center ecosystem' in the release.

original_interpretation: Deloitte estimates that about 1.05 trillion chips were sold in 2025 at an average selling price of US$0.74 per chip.
evidence_found: "In 2025, an estimated 1.05 trillion chips were sold at an average selling price of US$0.74 per chip." Endnote 7: "SIA estimates 1.05 trillion units of total chip sales for the full year 2025. Using WSTS's estimates of US$772 billion worth of total semiconductor industry revenue for 2025, the average selling price per unit comes to US$0.74."
correction: The 1.05 trillion units is SIA's estimate as relayed by Deloitte, not Deloitte's own. The US$0.74 ASP is Deloitte's division using WSTS's Dec-2025 forecast of US$772bn. On the final WSTS 2025 total of US$795.6bn (SRC-0428), the same unit count gives ~US$0.76 per chip.
notes: metric.methodology 'not disclosed' is wrong: endnote 7 discloses the method. The page has no visible date; its JSON-LD datePublished is 2026-02-04 (source publication_date patched).

original_interpretation: Deloitte estimates that generative-AI chips will be about 50% of industry revenue in 2026 but fewer than 20 million chips, roughly 0.2% of total unit volume.
evidence_found: "At a rough estimate, although gen AI chips are likely to account for about 50% of industry revenues in 2026, they are less than 20 million chips, or roughly 0.2% of total volume." Endnote 8: "...about 800,000 wafers ... about 20 chips per wafer, suggesting approximately 16 million chips ... the annual total number of AI chips produced could be about 20 million."
correction: Deloitte does say this, but its own inputs imply about 0.002%, not 0.2%: ~20 million gen-AI chips against the ~1.05 trillion total units it cites in endnote 7 (20e6/1.05e12 = 0.0019%). The intro's 'less than 0.2%' is technically true; 'roughly 0.2%' is off by about 100x. A corrected inference claim and a contradiction record were added.
notes: The arithmetic is mine, from the source's own endnotes 7 and 8. The unit counts mix years: 2025 total chips vs 2026 AI chips.

original_interpretation: Deloitte notes that while 2025 chip revenue was expected to rise 22%, silicon-wafer shipments rose only about 5.4%.
evidence_found: "Even though global chip revenues in 2025 are expected to rise 22%, silicon-wafer shipments increased by only an estimated 5.4% for the year." Endnote 9: SEMI forecast press release, Oct. 28, 2025. SEMI final, 10 Feb 2026: "Worldwide silicon wafer shipments in 2025 increased 5.8% to 12,973 million square inches (MSI)".
correction: The 5.4% was SEMI's Oct-2025 forecast. SEMI's year-end figure (SRC-0203, 10 Feb 2026) is +5.8% to 12,973 MSI (recorded as CLM-0522). The 22% revenue growth was also a forecast; the final WSTS 2025 growth was 26.2% (SRC-0428).
notes: The quote accurately reflects Deloitte. Both figures have been superseded by final data. No new claim was added because CLM-0522 already records the SEMI final figure.

original_interpretation: The OECD semiconductor taxonomy (August 2024) groups chips into four broad categories, logic, memory, analog and others, with sub-categories by prevalence, function and end use.
evidence_found: Executive summary (OECD 2024, PDF p. 6): "The taxonomy was developed by the Network and distinguishes semiconductor products into four broad categories – 'logic', 'memory', 'analog' and 'others' — and sub-categories based on their prevalence, specific functions and end-uses."
notes: The Foreword gives the same four categories but omits 'end-uses'. SRC-0431 is typed 'government'; OECD is an intergovernmental organisation, which is acceptable at tier 1.

original_interpretation: Unlike WSTS (which counts MPUs and MCUs as a separate 'micro' class), the OECD paper counts microprocessors (CPUs and GPUs), microcontrollers and connectivity chips as logic.
evidence_found: OECD (PDF p. 17): "Logic chips process binary information and include microprocessors (e.g. central processing units, CPUs and graphics processing units, GPUs), microcontrollers (MCUs) and connectivity chips." WSTS classification (p. 17): "P99 Total MOS Micro. Total of items P1, P2 (P51, P52 and P6) and P4."; p. 13: multi-core ICs "are NOT to be reported in this MOS Micro category, but ... under appropriate MOS Logic categories".
correction: The contrast holds for MPUs/CPUs and MCUs: WSTS puts them in a separate MOS Micro class (P1, P2, plus DSP P4), whereas OECD calls them logic. It does not cleanly hold for GPUs: WSTS has no GPU code, and ICs with multiple functional cores go to MOS Logic, so most GPUs/accelerators are already 'logic' in WSTS.
notes: The interpretation follows from the two quoted passages, apart from the GPU part.

original_interpretation: The OECD notes that most semiconductor demand analysis uses six end-use markets: computing/data processing, consumer goods, communications, automotive, industrial goods and government/military.
evidence_found: OECD 2024 (section 1, 'End-uses for semiconductors', PDF p. 10): "Generally, most analysis of semiconductor demand focuses on six main end-use markets: computing/data processing, consumer goods, communications, automotive, industrial goods, government/military."

original_interpretation: Micron's DRAM revenue rose 67% quarter-on-quarter in its fiscal Q3 2026: bit shipments rose in the low single digits, while average selling prices rose in the low-60s percent.
evidence_found: Micron FQ3-26 deck p. 22: "DRAM FQ3-26 • $31.3 billion, representing 76% of total revenue in FQ3-26 • Revenue increased 67% Q/Q • Bit shipments up low-single digit percentage range Q/Q • ASPs increased in low-60s percentage range Q/Q"; p. 34 table: DRAM $31,328 vs $18,768 (67%). Micron FQ4 release table: '3rd Qtr. May 28, 2026'.
notes: The quarter-end date of 28 May 2026 is confirmed by Micron's FQ4-26 press release column header (opened; not added as a source). metric.value 60 stands in for the 'low-60s' range.

original_interpretation: Micron's NAND revenue rose 99% quarter-on-quarter in fiscal Q3 2026: bit shipments rose in the mid single digits, while average selling prices rose in the mid-80s percent.
evidence_found: Micron FQ3-26 deck p. 22: "NAND FQ3-26 • $9.9 billion, representing 24% of total revenue in FQ3-26 • Revenue increased 99% Q/Q • Bit shipments increased in mid-single digit percentage range Q/Q • ASPs increased in mid-80s percentage range Q/Q"; p. 34: NAND 9,943 vs 4,997 (99%).
notes: metric.value 85 stands in for the 'mid-80s' range.

original_interpretation: Micron expects industry DRAM bit shipments to grow in the low-to-mid 20s percent and NAND bit shipments about 20% in calendar 2026.
evidence_found: FQ3-26 deck p. 16 (24 Jun 2026): "industry DRAM bit shipments in calendar 2026 to grow in the low- to mid-20s percentage range"; "industry NAND bit shipments in calendar 2026 to grow approximately 20%". FQ4-26 deck p. 16 (30 Sep 2026): "In NAND, for calendar 2026, we expect industry bit shipments to grow in the low-20s percentage range, slightly above our prior expectations."; "In DRAM ... mid-20s percentage range."
correction: Micron updated these on 30 Sep 2026 (FQ4-26 deck, p. 16): CY2026 industry DRAM bit shipments now grow in the mid-20s percent, and NAND in the low-20s percent ('slightly above our prior expectations'). It also guides CY2027-28 at roughly low-20s (DRAM) and mid-20s (NAND).
notes: The original was accurate as of 24 Jun 2026. Superseding claims were added.

original_interpretation: In 2Q26 TSMC's net revenue by platform was high-performance computing 66%, smartphone 22%, IoT 5%, automotive 4%, digital consumer electronics 1% and others 2%.
evidence_found: TSMC 2Q26 Management Report p. 2: "By platform, HPC and Smartphone represented 66% and 22% of net revenue respectively, while IoT, Automotive, DCE, and Others each represented 5%, 4%, 1%, and 2%."; table 'Net Revenue by Platform' 2Q26: HPC 66%, Smartphone 22%, IoT 5%, Automotive 4%, DCE 1%, Others 2%.
notes: Opened with web_extract. The browser was blocked by a Cloudflare check.

original_interpretation: In 2Q26, 3nm contributed 30%, 5nm 33%, 7nm 11% and 2nm 3% of TSMC wafer revenue; 7nm and below totalled 77%.
evidence_found: TSMC 2Q26 Management Report p. 2: "By technology, 2nm process technology contributed 3% of total wafer revenue in 2Q26, while 3nm, 5nm, and 7nm accounted for 30%, 33%, and 11% respectively. Advanced technologies (7nm and below) accounted for 77% of total wafer revenue."

original_interpretation: TSMC's HPC revenue grew 20% quarter-on-quarter in 2Q26 while smartphone revenue fell 4%.
evidence_found: TSMC 2Q26 Management Report p. 2: "Sequentially, revenue from HPC, IoT, Automotive, DCE, and Others increased 20%, 4%, 15%, 5%, and 5% respectively. Smartphone decreased 4% from 1Q26."
